readerTitle: Thirty charts lost. One sentence won.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (사무실 청소 회사, 배관 업체) + 실제 연구 (Gigerenzer 등의 자연 빈도 연구) · 모든 사업 수치는 설명용
insight: 숫자는 많이 보여줄수록 설득되는 게 아니다. 비교 기준과 '그래서 무엇이 달라지나'가 붙은 숫자 하나가 이야기를 만든다.
misconception: 데이터를 많이, 빠짐없이 보여주면 상대가 알아서 같은 결론에 도달한다.

sources.text: Gigerenzer, G. & Hoffrage, U. (1995). How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: Frequency formats. Psychological Review, 102(4).
Hoffrage, U. & Gigerenzer, G. (1998). Using natural frequencies to improve diagnostic inferences. Academic Medicine, 73(5).
청소 회사와 배관 업체의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 5번 카드의 연구 요약(백분율보다 '1,000명 중 10명' 같은 자연 빈도로 제시할 때 의사를 포함한 사람들의 확률 추론이 크게 좋아짐)을 원 논문으로 다시 확인하세요. 구체적 정답률 수치는 일부러 넣지 않았습니다.
청소 회사 계산: 누락 청소 월 2건 → 11건, 늘어난 9건 × 건당 보상 크레딧 $300 = 월 $2,700. 차트 값(1~6월: 2, 3, 2, 6, 9, 11)은 가상 수치입니다.
배관 업체 계산: 월 작업 약 325건 × 재방문율 8% = 26건(근무일 기준 거의 하루 1건). 26건 × 무급 2시간 = 52시간 > 주 40시간. 재방문율 6.1% → 8.0%는 상대 증가 1.9 ÷ 6.1 = 약 31%.

cards.title: Thirty charts lost. One sentence won.
body: An operations lead at an office-cleaning company sent her partner a 30-chart report. It made the case for hiring a second crew. The partner skimmed it and said no.
A week later she sent one sentence with three numbers in it. He said yes the same afternoon. The data hadn't changed. The story had.

image.label: A tall stack of charts next to a single note card
image.brief: 책상 위 왼쪽에는 차트가 인쇄된 종이가 높이 쌓여 있고 먼지가 앉아 있음. 오른쪽에는 숫자 세 개만 적힌 작은 메모 카드 한 장에 조명이 비침. 따뜻한 플랫 일러스트, 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Which message gets the crew approved?
body: You run operations at an office-cleaning firm. Since you took on a big new contract, crews are stretched. You want your partner to approve a second van crew.
Which message would you send?

options.text: A full dashboard: hours, jobs, complaints, overtime, supplies and twelve other metrics
options.feedback: Nothing is hidden, but nothing stands out. Your partner has to find the problem and the conclusion alone, and most readers won't.

options.text: "Complaints are up 40%. We need another crew."
options.feedback: Short and clear, but 40% of what? Up from 5 to 7 sounds very different from 50 to 70, and it doesn't say what it costs.

options.text: "Missed cleanings went from 2 a month to 11 since the new contract. The extra misses cost $2,700 a month in credits, and our biggest client renews in March."
options.feedback: One number, a clear before and after, a cost and a deadline. It takes more work to write, but the reader sees the decision at once.

cards.title: The warning was in the report. It just didn't speak.
body: In the 30-chart version, missed cleanings sat on page 17, next to supply costs and staff hours. Most charts were steady, so the report felt fine.
The one line that mattered looked like this. Nobody told the partner to look at it, or why it mattered.

cards.title: Telling a story with numbers
body: A number alone is just a fact. It becomes a story when it answers two questions: **compared to what?** and **so what?**
"11 missed cleanings" is a fact. "Up from 2" gives the comparison. "$2,700 a month, and a renewal at risk" says why it matters for the decision.
Pick the one number that carries the argument. Give it a comparison and a consequence. Everything else becomes backup.

image.label: A number linked to a comparison and a consequence
image.brief: 가로 흐름 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "11" 큰 숫자 → 가운데 "compared to 2" → 오른쪽 "$2,700/month + renewal at risk". 각 칸 아래에 작은 라벨 "Number", "Compared to what?", "So what?". 단순한 선과 두 가지 색만 사용.

cards.title: The same fact, framed differently, gets understood differently.
body: Psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer and colleagues gave people, including doctors, the same medical test data in two forms. One used percentages. The other used counts like "10 out of 1,000 people."
With counts, far more people reached the right answer. The facts were identical. The format decided whether they made sense.
The lesson for business: translate numbers into units your reader can picture. "About one missed office every other workday" lands faster than "a 450% increase."

cards.title: Good comparisons come in a few shapes.
body: Most strong number stories use one of these anchors. Choose the one your reader already cares about.
list: **Before and after:** last quarter versus this one
**Against a target:** what we promised versus what we did
**Against a cost they know:** "about the price of one part-time hire"
**Against a deadline:** "the client renews in March"
cards.softwareNote: "Monthly churn is 4%" rarely moves a room. "We lose about 1 in 25 customers every month, roughly half of what sales brings in" makes the leak visible and points to a decision.

cards.title: Choosing the comparison is a choice. Readers know it.
body: The same data can tell opposite stories. Pick a lucky starting month or a relative change on a tiny base, and you can make almost anything look like a crisis or a win.
A good story should survive the full data. Keep the backup ready, and say which number would change your mind.
If a skeptic finds the chart you left out, you lose more than the argument. You lose trust in your next number too.

cards.title: Now it's a plumbing business.
body: You own a plumbing company with eight plumbers. You want them to use a five-minute checklist before leaving each job. The problem is callbacks: return visits to fix your own work. They're 8% of jobs, up from 6.1% last year.
How do you open the team meeting?

options.feedback: Accurate, but with no comparison or consequence it sounds small. Most of the team will nod and move on.

options.text: "Last month we went back to 26 finished jobs, almost one a day. At two unpaid hours each, that's more than a full week of one plumber's time."
options.feedback: A count they can picture, tied to time they all feel. The checklist now looks cheap next to the problem.
It's dramatic and true, but a relative change hides the base. Someone will do the math, find it's under two points, and stop trusting the rest.

cards.softwareNote: The same move works for bug reports: "40 tickets last month from one release, about two days of support time" beats "defect rate up 0.3%."

cards.title: One number, compared to something, with a "so what."
body: More data doesn't persuade on its own. Pick the number that carries the decision, anchor it to a comparison your reader cares about, and say what it changes.
**Try it today:** take one number from your next report. Rewrite it as one sentence with a comparison and a consequence.
